articles.summary: President Donald Trump arrives in the Philippines ahead of a historic summit with China's Xi Jinping, following bruising GOP losses in the U.S. midterm elections.
articles.body: President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday as part of an Asia trip that will take him to China for a historic summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The trip marks Trump's first overseas visit since Republicans suffered bruising defeats in the U.S. midterm elections. Trump noted during a gaggle on Monday that while in China this week he will meet with Chinese President Xi Jingping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS "And then we go to China. And we'll be with President Xi, he was here a month ago. And we're also gonna meet with President Putin. And we may meet with Kim Jong Un also," Trump said, referring to North Korea's leader. "He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump later added. Trump indicated that during the meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, they would discuss issues including denuclearization, Iran, Ukraine, economics and trade. TRUMP'S ASIA TRIP TAKES ALASKA DETOUR AS WEATHER FORCES REFUELING STOP CHANGE The trip also comes after tech giant Nvidia announced last week that President and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from the company — the resignation announcement was made after Huang admitted to cheating on his wife amid reporting that he had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. articles.title: Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?
articles.summary: Votes are still being counted in the Alaska Senate race, with Democrat Mary Peltola ahead of Republican incumbent Senator Dan S Sullivan.
articles.body:
Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.

This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".

US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.

But with 98% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.

Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.

BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.

The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.

This calls into question claims that Republican voters may have been confused about which Sullivan they were voting for.

How did two Dan Sullivans end up in the race?

Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term.

Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign.

A New York Times story published the week before Election Day claimed that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

The report said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.

Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.

President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".

But experts note it's not an illegal tactic, if it was employed.

"There is nothing to prevent a campaign from recruiting someone else to run, even if for political reasons," said Joshua Douglas, an election law expert at the University of Kentucky.

Voters in Alaska select their first choice candidate, followed by options to rank up to four other candidates in order of preference.

"There is no specific law preventing people with the same name running, but many states have laws or regulations about how names appear on the ballot. One of those regulations was used in Alaska" said Ruth Greenwood, director of the election law clinic at Harvard Law School.

On Alaskans' ballots the two Sullivans were listed as:

Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent

There was a second registered Republican candidate, Gerald Heikes - who was also allegedly recruited into the race according to The New York Times.

As of Tuesday, Peltola holds 49.98% of the vote.

In the event that Peltola were not to clear 50%, officials eliminate the candidate in last place and reallocate those ballots to the voters' next choices. This process continues until two candidates remain, with one clearing the 50% hurdle.

Daniel J Sullivan Jr is the listed candidate in last place with 1.65% of the vote.

What does ranked-choice voting data show so far?

Senator Dan S Sullivan and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.

Trump said last week: "Anybody that voted for that second Dan Sullivan, the fake Dan Sullivan, was supposed to be a vote for the real Dan Sullivan".

Of the ballots analysed by BBC Verify that ranked Daniel J Sullivan Jr first, 38% of them recorded no valid second choice.

We do not know how many of these voters may have thought they had voted for the Senator Dan S Sullivan and then not ranked any other candidates.

A further 29% of Daniel J Sullivan Jr voters ranked the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola second, almost double the 15% that ranked the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan as second.

"The likelihood that any confusion might play a significant role is diminished in Alaska," Richard Pildes, a professor of constitutional law at New York University, argues, "because any voter who was unsure which Dan Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for could rank them first and second."

Additional reporting by Daniel Wainwright

articles.title: Buttigieg trashes Duffy’s ground stop response, but his DOT failures doom his 2028 bid
articles.summary: Pete Buttigieg's criticism of Sean Duffy's airline ground stop response is backfiring, reviving scrutiny of his supply chain absence and #WheresPete era.
articles.body: Seeking attention and perhaps absolution, presidential wannabe Pete Buttigieg threw himself into the controversy over last week’s airline ground stop; it did not go well. The former secretary of transportation desperately wants to be taken seriously as a 2028 candidate but is struggling to gain much of a following, currently ranking fifth in surveys of potential Democratic contenders. Maybe that’s because most people remember what a lousy job he did during the Biden years, a record he is foolishly inviting us to review. Sensing an opportunity to make headlines and rewrite his history, Buttigieg was quick to criticize Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s press conference about the shutdown of our airports, saying, "You can just write down the comic book asterisk swearing characters." BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS And then Buttigieg held a press conference, claiming he was "like everyone else, very concerned about what's going on in the national airspace." He acknowledged he had no "inside knowledge" about what was happening and therefore had nothing to say. If Duffy’s presser was insufficient, Pete’s was pointless. Pete goofed. By piling on his successor during the shutdown, Buttigieg is reminding us of his own shortcomings as transportation secretary, his only credential even remotely deserving of a promotion to the White House. Unfortunately for Pete, his Cabinet term is widely considered to have been a disaster, best known for his eight-week disappearance at the peak of a critical supply chain shortage brought on by COVID-19. With hundreds of ships lined up at the nation’s ports unable to unload cargo, and goods of all kinds running out as Christmas loomed, AWOL Buttigieg earned #WheresPete mockery on Twitter. Turns out, the former South Bend mayor was home enjoying an extended family leave (he and his partner adopted twins who were born prematurely). Finally outed by Politico, Pete returned — not to work opening up the ports and solving other supply bottlenecks — but to a heavy schedule of media appearances. Unapologetic about his absence and devoid of solutions to the supply chain crunch, the secretary blamed consumers for an excess of demand, even as he pushed for more of Biden’s mammoth spending bills that fueled the shortages in the first place. Among other snafus on Pete’s watch, there was indeed a nationwide ground stop, the first since the security-related shutdown following the terrorist attacks on 9/11. The 2023 halt to air travel lasted around 90 minutes and was caused by the failure of a system meant to alert pilots to hazards such as closed runways. FAA GROUND STOP TIMELINE: WEEKEND CHAOS GROUNDS PLANES AND POSTPONES GAMES That breakdown was one of many signals that our decrepit air traffic system needed repair — repair that Buttigieg neglected to provide. As Duffy posted on X: "Mayor Pete failed for four years to address the air traffic controller shortage and upgrade our outdated, World War II-era air traffic control system." According to Duffy, DEI-obsessed Buttigieg bungled efforts to expand the number of air traffic controllers in part by lowering the acceptance requirements for training, leading to delays in the process and a surge in dropout rates at the FAA Academy in Oklahoma City. In less than two years, Duffy turned around the program; as a result, the FAA announced last month that it exceeded its fiscal 2026 goal by hiring 2,235 air traffic controller trainees, the most in FAA history. FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP Buttigieg weakened the credentials needed to become an air traffic controller in a search for a more diverse pool of candidates. Like most of the Biden administration, he prioritized equity and diversity in the FAA trainee pool over building up the capabilities of the critical industry. But it wasn’t only racial diversity he pursued. In 2024, Fox News reported that "the Federal Aviation Administration is actively recruiting workers who suffer ‘severe intellectual’ disabilities, psychiatric problems and other mental and physical conditions under a diversity and inclusion hiring initiative spelled out on the agency’s website." Should Pete run for president, critics will question this initiative. They will also wonder why only $5 billion of the $25 billion allocated to the FAA under the bipartisan infrastructure law went toward upgrading air traffic control towers and systems. EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP'S FAA TOUTS NEW AI-POWERED TOOL HELPING THOUSANDS OF PASSENGERS AVOID FLIGHT DELAYS Voters may also question the sluggish pace of the administration's $7.5 billion electric vehicle charging initiative. While the 2021 infrastructure law aimed to catalyze a nationwide network of 500,000 public chargers by 2030 alongside private industry, bureaucratic hurdles and state-by-state permitting slowed the federal rollout to a crawl. Two and a half years after the bill passed, left-wing CBS’s Margaret Brennan pressed Buttigieg on "Face the Nation" over why only eight federally funded stations had actually come online — raising legitimate questions about whether federal red tape and domestic-sourcing mandates bogged down a signature transportation priority. And then there was Pete’s special effort to "fix" our highway system, described by this NPR headline: "Pete Buttigieg launches $1B pilot to build racial equity in America's roads." The program, derided by Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis as the "woke-ification" of federal policy, was designed to "rectify harm caused by roadways that were built primarily through lower-income, Black communities after the 1950s creation of the interstate highway system." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Returning to the recent airspace closure, Pete tried to evade responsibility for our dilapidated FAA systems and rebuke Duffy, saying during a press availability on Nov. 13 that was carried on C-SPAN, "We did a lot to upgrade the system. When we had an outage, I didn't stand there complaining about the Trump administration. We got to work ... I'm certain that that's what career officials ... at FAA and USDOT are doing. This should not be about politics." But Pete didn’t get to work. In 2024, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported: "FAA determined that 51 of its 138 systems are unsustainable, citing outdated functionality, a lack of spare parts, and more. Over half of these unsustainable systems are especially concerning, but FAA has been slow to modernize. Some system modernization projects won't be complete for another 10–13 years. FAA also doesn't have plans to modernize other systems in need — 3 of which are at least 30 years old." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Buttigieg was too busy worrying about racist roads to fix our FAA, leaving Duffy a broken system which he is attempting to modernize. Yes, Pete, you’re right: It’s not about politics; it’s about performance. Too bad yours will keep you far, far away from the White House. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM LIZ PEEK

articles.title: Trump kicks off high-stakes Asia trip with Xi, Putin meetings looming on world stage
articles.summary: President Donald Trump is set to sign a trade deal with Thailand at the ASEAN summit before heading to China for historic talks with Xi Jinping.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is in Asia for historic talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin this week, with nuclear arms reductions and Iran on the agenda and Trump signaling Monday that he also plans to raise Russia's war in Ukraine. Trump's trip began Tuesday in the Philippines at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit before he travels to Shenzhen, China, for Thursday's meeting with Xi and Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. The rare gathering comes amid simmering U.S.-China trade tensions and ongoing conflicts involving Russia and Iran, with Trump signaling plans to raise denuclearization and efforts to end the fighting. At the ASEAN summit, Trump is expected to sign a joint statement with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul announcing progress toward a trade agreement. The president is also set to meet with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. before departing for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA The president has also raised the possibility of meeting with North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un during his visit to China this week, telling reporters Monday that talks could take place. When reached for additional comment about the floated meeting, the White House referred Fox News Digital to Trump's remarks to reporters on Monday. Trump is expected to discuss Iran and Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during Thursday's highly-anticipated trilateral meeting, despite U.S. officials previously telling ABC News that Ukraine likely would not be on the agenda. Trump notably told reporters on Nov. 8 that he plans to discuss denuclearization and ending the war in Iran during the trilateral meeting, DW News reported. "We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we'll be talking a lot of things. We're trying to end the war in Iran," the president said at the time. Trump's trip also comes amid a scandal involving Nvidia, the American tech giant whose powerful AI chips are at the center of growing tensions between the U.S. and China. Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned last week following reports of an affair with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of sharing information with Beijing, raising fresh concerns about Chinese espionage and access to sensitive American technology. Trump cast doubt on the espionage allegations Monday, telling reporters he was unsure whether the woman was a Chinese spy. He also said he would be open to Huang returning as CEO. TRUMP-XI REUNION COMES WITH UNFINISHED BUSINESS — AND A BIGGER BATTLE LOOMING The president will be joined by several high-profile figures during his Asia trip, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is accompanying Trump to the Philippines and China this week, according to Rubio's public schedule. Tesla CEO Elon Musk is also expected to join Trump for part of his trip to China for the APEC summit, U.S. officials confirmed to CNBC on Friday. Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chairman of the House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, told CBS News’ "Face the Nation" in an interview on Sunday that he does not anticipate any agreements related to the reduction of nuclear weapons will be made this week. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I don’t believe any agreements are going to be made, but certainly China has resisted being part of any agreements," Moolenaar told CBS News. "And if there’s a way to provide more security for the American people through those kinds of discussions, I think it’s important to have it." Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

articles.title: I talked with Trump. Will his final years lead to an immigration deal?
articles.summary: Trump signals he's open to negotiating regularization for nonviolent immigrants but warns Democrats that impeachment efforts could kill any deal.
articles.body: It is test time again for Democrats. They know how to campaign against President Donald Trump when he is not on the ballot for the presidency. But does the Democratic Party actually want to accomplish something for immigrants who are in the country illegally? Many of their candidates swept in by the blue tsunami of two weeks ago, campaigned on helping the millions of immigrants who entered the country illegally during President Joe Biden’s term. But will they deliver that group … anything? Because if the Democrats actually want to do that, Trump is ready to begin negotiations. TRUMP OPENS DOOR TO IMMIGRATION DEAL, BUT REPUBLICANS HAVE ONE CONDITION If the Democrats actually wanted to accomplish something for immigrants who are in the United States without the legal right to be here, the new speaker of the House and the new majority leader in the Senate could present Trump many different and acceptable pieces of legislation addressing some or all of those immigrants. If the proposals are reasonable, a genuine negotiation would follow between the president and the Democratic majorities over what they both wanted, and each could get most of what they want done. If Democrats want a blanket amnesty, that won’t work. If they demand a "path to citizenship and voting," that would be a bridge too far. But if they seek "regularization" of people who are nonviolent and willing to work? TRUMP TELLS DHS CHIEF TO WORK WITH DEMOCRATS ON IMMIGRATION REFORM, BUT NO AMNESTY On Thursday, I asked Trump: "If Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer come up, and they want the DREAMers, or they want regularization for people who aren’t violent in the country, what are you going to want?" The president didn’t respond directly to that hypothetical, but instead suggested there was room to negotiate on healthcare issues. "[G]reat things can be done between the Democrats and the Republicans on healthcare," Trump said. "And if I can do that with the Democrats, I’d love to do that." DEMOCRATS PLOT MASSIVE SPENDING SPREE AFTER MIDTERM ROUT — AND TRUMP COULD HELP THEM PULL IT OFF That exchange followed the president laying out a "condition precedent" of sorts (the legal term for an event or requirement that must occur or be satisfied before a contractual obligation becomes enforceable, or a party is required to perform its side of any deal). "So you can negotiate," I observed to the president. "But if they’re impeaching you, can you negotiate with the Democrats if they’re trying to destroy you at the same time?" TRUMP SAYS HE 'CAN'T IMAGINE' DEMOCRATS WILL IMPEACH HIM A THIRD TIME "Maybe not," the president replied. "Maybe I wouldn’t want to, because it’s in such bad, you know, when I negotiate, I negotiate in good faith. If they’re doing that, it’s in bad faith." So, quite simply, every potential subject of legislation, including "regularization" of millions of illegal immigrants, is on the table when the new Congress arrives, but the table itself vanishes if the Democrats want to investigate rather than legislate. THE MISTAKE NEWLY-ELECTED DEMS ADMIT THEY CAN'T AFFORD TO MAKE WITH TRUMP AFTER SWEEPING 2026 WINS That’s a reasonable position from the president, but it is hard to see the incoming wave of democratic socialists, plus "the Squad" in the House agreeing to anything that could be termed a compromise, no matter the upside for the immigrant community. If Democrats want a blanket amnesty, that won’t work. If they demand a "path to citizenship and voting," that would be a bridge too far. But if they seek "regularization" of people who are nonviolent and willing to work? To get to a deal, the "get Trump" Democrats would have to set aside their deep desire to grandstand so that they could accomplish some sort of security for the 10 to 20 million immigrants in the United States who are in danger of deportation if they cross the path of ICE. AT LEAST 9 NEW DEM MEMBERS WILL CARRY AL GREEN'S MANTLE AND TRY TO IMPEACH PRESIDENT TRUMP Which is why the immigrant communities have their hopes up. The goal of the conditional right to remain — a felony conviction would of course end a conditional visa — is within reach. But such hopes were dashed by President Barack Obama when he had his large majorities in both the House and the Senate in January 2009, and again by Biden in January 2021 when he was supported by majorities in both houses of Congress. Both men abandoned this constituency. JEFFRIES PROMISES ‘REMEDIAL ASSISTANCE’ TO ANYONE IMPACTED BY TRUMP IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT Because being a Democratic leader means never having to say you are sorry to the people who trusted you. Immigrants should not get their hopes up, as Democrats have a record of amnesia about them when they have legislative majorities. Which is why the exile the GOP is about to enter in Congress isn’t remotely permanent or even likely to be long. Democrats have proven incapable in the past two decades of actually delivering anything for their coalition partners. Their big achievements? Obamacare under Obama and a flood of spending under Biden. The former wrecked healthcare delivery in the U.S., and the latter ignited the inflation which remains between 3% and 4%, that, while much lower now than its peak in the Biden years, is still the primary reason the GOP got the boot on Nov. 3. Democrats have a short window in which to prove to the voters who are "up for grabs" — immigrants and their extended families, friends and communities — that it won’t be a "third strike." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION President Trump will want something in return for his signature, and that is most likely funding for the "Golden Dome," a U.S. missile defense system, and the Golden Fleet, which includes plans for nuclear-powered guided-missile warships. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Will the Democrats actually deliver? Doubtful, but perhaps their youngest elected members of the House and Senate will urge them to turn from the impossible-to-win battles for impeachment to the real stuff of legislative accomplishment. articles.title: Schumer boasts early advantage in Senate power struggle as Dem rival warns against 'coronation'
articles.summary: Senate Democrats face their first leadership race in decades as Chris Van Hollen alleges the Dec. 1 secret ballot vote may be rushed to kneecap him.
articles.body: With a historic race to be the top Senate Democrat locked in, both candidates eyeing the job of leading Democrats into their majority believe they have a path to victory. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., has raised a challenge to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to steer Democrats through the final two years of President Donald Trump’s time in office. It’s the first time in three decades that the race has been contested, and both believe they have or can get the 28 votes needed to claim the mantle of Democratic leader and become majority leader. But neither has publicly locked down enough support to eclipse the magic number. DEMOCRATS TURN ON SCHUMER AFTER HISTORIC ELECTION WINS AS POTENTIAL CHALLENGER EMERGES Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade as both minority and majority leader, so far has 15 senators in his camp, making him the clear front-runner. The longtime Democratic leader has remained confident, but quiet, about his chances of retaining his job, posting shortly after Van Hollen’s announcement last week that he welcomed "discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead," but asserted, "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader." Schumer’s allies, like Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., argue that he has led Senate Democrats to a 55-seat majority, which could expand by another seat if Alaska flips. CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER' Van Hollen, who acknowledged that he is the "underdog," has five public backers who can vote in the forthcoming leadership elections — Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., who is retiring, is backing Van Hollen but doesn’t have a vote. His base of support includes Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who caucuses with Senate Democrats, Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, both progressives whom Schumer did not initially back in their respective races. Van Hollen, however, argued that he has as many as 15 in his corner. He also alleged in an interview with Politico that Democrats were trying to move up the Dec. 1 secret-ballot leadership election to kneecap his chances. "Let’s not rush into a coronation," Van Hollen said. Fox News Digital reached out for comment from Van Hollen and Schumer’s offices about Van Hollen's claim. SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED While Schumer is playing the quiet game, Van Hollen has launched a public push for the job, making several appearances across the gamut of cable news and launching his own website declaring that voters’ backing of Democrats across the country was a rejection of the "status quo," and that "to deliver, we need new leadership." There’s also a request for donations on the site, raising questions about Van Hollen’s future ambitions. He initially was "kicking the tires" on a 2028 bid for the White House, but since then, he has dropped the idea. Just a week earlier, Van Hollen was mulling higher office, but now he’s giving up a potential bid for the White House in 2028 to do one thing: beat Schumer and grapple with President Donald Trump. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I’m no longer pursuing that," Van Hollen told reporters at the What’s Next conference in Denver. But it raises the question whether a leadership bid is a launch pad for higher office. "At a minimum, it’s good for his base fundraising," a Democratic source told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Marcos Llorente responde a Pablo Bustinduy por las propuestas de Frente Amplio: “Ahora van a decidir cuánto de lo que has construido en tu vida vas a dejar a tus hijos”
articles.standfirst: El futbolista del Atlético de Madrid responde en Instagram a la medida sobre las grandes herencias
articles.summary: El futbolista del Atlético de Madrid responde en Instagram a la medida sobre las grandes herencias
articles.body: El futbolista del Atlético de Madrid, Marcos Llorente, ha reaccionado a la propuesta del Frente Amplio de limitar las grandes herencias. Lo hizo en Instagram comentando un video de Pablo Bustinduy publicado por la cuenta de Wall Street Wolverine en el que el ministro propone gravar el 100% de la parte de cada herencia que supere los diez millones de euros por heredero. El centrocampista rojiblanco pregunta si la Administración puede limitar la transferencia de la riqueza familiar. Llorente dijo en su comentario: "Ahora el Estado va a decidir cuánto de lo que construiste durante tu vida tienes derecho a dejar a tus hijos". Luego añadió: "Y el resto se lo quedan" y terminó con la frase "Tócate los huevos". La iniciativa forma parte del programa electoral del Frente Amplio. Propone aplicar la tasa máxima sólo sobre lo que exceda los 10 millones de euros por beneficiario (no sobre toda la herencia). Cabe destacar que es una propuesta electoral y no una normativa en vigor. En el video que desencadenó esta respuesta, Bustinduy dice: “Nadie en España va a heredar más de lo que puede gastar en una vida”. El ministro defiende que debería gastarse en servicios públicos que son “el patrimonio de todos los demás”. Bustinduy atribuye la iniciativa a la desigualdad de oportunidades y compara la riqueza heredada con el dinero ganado a través del trabajo: “No puedes nacer con más dinero del que puedes ganar en una vida trabajando”, dice. También cuestiona el mérito asociado a la riqueza familiar: “¿De qué hay que estar orgulloso por haber nacido en una familia rica? ¿Qué apellido vale diez millones de euros?” El video reafirma la posición del ministro y ha llevado el debate sobre la fiscalidad de las herencias a los comentarios de la publicación. La medida se sitúa en el debate sobre la concentración de grandes fortunas y la fiscalidad de las herencias. Su eventual aplicación tendría que especificar cuestiones como la valoración de los bienes heredados y su encaje con las competencias regionales en materia de impuesto de sucesiones.

articles.title: Is Pakistan about to carve out new provinces? Inside the controversial plan
articles.summary: Talk of new provinces has gathered pace, but there is no formal proposal or agreement among governing parties.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Pakistan’s defence minister has said the country could have multiple new provinces as early as the New Year.

“My own view is that New Year will see this, the new system also, God willing,” Khwaja Asif told a private news channel programme this week.

Asif, a senior leader of the governing Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) party, was discussing proposals to carve new provinces out of the existing four: Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and Balochistan.

But Asif stressed that he was offering his own assessment. “I have no inside information at this time, and even if I did, obviously I cannot spill it over on a show,” he said.

Nearly four months after Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi first pitched the idea publicly, the proposal appears to be gaining steam. Yet no draft constitutional amendment, agreed number of provinces or timetable have been made public.

Here is what we know about the proposal, the constitutional process, the referendum being discussed to implement it and the concerns raised by political parties:

At an economic summit in Islamabad on July 30, Naqvi, considered a close confidant of military chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, said Pakistan needed new administrative units to improve governance.

“Unless units are made and they take ownership and a new leadership comes, this will not happen,” he said.

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal has spoken of 12 to 15 provinces to be created through consensus.

Supporters argue that the four provinces are too large to deliver services effectively to a population of about 250 million and a constitutional amendment in 2010 aimed at decentralising powers and resources to districts and cities has not been effective.

“Powers and resources were taken in the name of the people and parked in the chief minister’s house. That is exactly why there is talk of smaller administrative units,” Mustafa Kamal, the federal health minister and a leader of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P), Sindh’s second-largest party, said in television interviews this week.

But Kamal said the federal cabinet had not formally discussed the matter. Asked how many new units were planned, he said he did not know.

“I am also hearing all these things, watching everything, but officially I do not know at all,” he said.

Malik Ahmad Khan, the Punjab Assembly speaker and a PML-N leader, told Al Jazeera that Asif had not explained his timeline.

Kamal, however, pointed to the political calendar: Elections for the Senate, the upper chamber of Pakistan’s Parliament, are due early next year, followed by the federal budget.

“December is a very important month. There are Senate elections ahead. After that, the budget will come in June, so whatever has to happen has to happen before that,” he said.

Pakistan’s Constitution recognises four provinces but has no separate procedure for creating new ones. The debate, therefore, centres on Article 239, which governs constitutional amendments.

An amendment requires two-thirds of the total membership of each house of parliament: 224 of the 336 National Assembly members and 64 of the 96 senators.

Under Article 239(4), an amendment changing a province’s boundaries must also win two-thirds support in that province’s assembly before it goes to the president for assent. That would require, for example, 248 of the 371 members in the Punjab Assembly and 112 of the 168 in the Provincial Assembly of Sindh.

“With this specific system in place in the constitution”, no other “route can be used” to try to carve out provinces, Abdul Moiz Jaferii, a Karachi-based constitutional lawyer, told Al Jazeera.

There has been an earlier attempt. In May 2012, the Punjab Assembly unanimously adopted two resolutions moved by Rana Sanaullah, the then-provincial law minister and now an adviser to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, calling for a South Punjab province and the restoration of Bahawalpur province.

In March 2013, the Senate passed a constitutional amendment bill to create a Bahawalpur Janoobi Punjab province.

But it lapsed days later when the National Assembly’s term ended without the lower house taking it up.

Jaferii also questioned whether creating new provinces would necessarily improve governance.

“New provinces would not in and of themselves make government work better. They would allow for smaller administrative units, which in theory are easier to manage. But these units can be achieved without constitutional tinkering with provincial boundaries,” he said.

Last week, Naqvi told reporters in Lahore that the question of creating new provinces should be put to the public.

“If the people say they should not be made, I am 100 percent with them that they should not be made. If the people say they should be made, then let them be made,” he said.

Article 48(6) of the constitution allows the prime minister to refer a matter of national importance to a joint sitting of parliament.

If the joint session approves it, the matter could go to a referendum that poses a “yes” or “no” question to voters. But legal experts said a referendum’s outcome is not binding on the government.

Malik said the route was legitimate and elected representatives could not disregard the public’s decision.

“Now if the government decides that it has to go to Article 48 and first take the opinion of the public and present before parliament what question they frame, then this is also their right and very much constitutional,” he told Al Jazeera.

Kamal said a referendum remained an option if parties could not agree on an amendment.

Jaferii, however, said a referendum could not replace the constitutional amendment process.

“A referendum cannot be used as a substitute to such a specifically delineated process, nor do referenda allow for the asking of anything but a binary question from the population as a whole, the answer to which is not binding upon those asking it,” he said.

Pakistan has held three referendums, each under a military ruler.

In 1960, about 80,000 local councillors, known as Basic Democrats, were asked whether they had confidence in Ayub Khan, the country’s military ruler and its first field marshal. They said they did.

In 1984, voters were asked whether they endorsed General Zia-ul-Haq’s Islamisation programme with a “yes” counted as a vote for him to stay on as president for five more years.

In 2002, General Pervez Musharraf used one to secure a five-year presidential term.

“Referendum is not a first option – referendum is a second option, just like we have governor rule, emergency clauses in the constitution, but they are not there to be applied regularly, normally,” Majid Nizami, a Lahore-based political analyst, told Al Jazeera.

How much would new provinces cost, and what about money and water?

Currently, Pakistan’s provinces receive 57.5 percent of the federal pool of taxes. This financial year, that amounts to 8.64 trillion rupees ($31.2bn).

Punjab receives 51.74 percent of the provincial share, Sindh 24.55 percent, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 14.62 percent and Balochistan 9.09 percent. What they get is proportionate to their populations.

However, the constitution does not specify how an existing province’s share should be divided among any new provinces created from it.

The Islamabad-based Policy Research Institute of Market Economy (PRIME) estimated in October that dividing Punjab into three provinces would cost 46.9 billion to 56.2 billion rupees ($169m to $203m) a year.

A stress-test scenario in which all 30 of Pakistan’s divisions became provinces would cost 609.2 billion to 730.3 billion rupees ($2.2bn to $2.64bn), PRIME estimated.

The estimates excluded one-off set-up costs, police forces and full secretariats. PRIME also said equal Senate representation for each province would increase the upper house from 96 to 142 seats if Punjab alone were divided.

Water remains a question too. The 1991 Water Apportionment Accord, which allocates Indus River system water among the four provinces, is not part of the constitution. None of the proposals made public so far has explained how water or financial resources would be shared among any new provinces.

Syed Nasir Hussain Shah, Sindh’s local government minister and deputy general secretary of the Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) in Sindh, said Pakistan’s economy could not bear the cost of additional assemblies, secretariats, chief minister and governor houses, and courts.

“Is making provinces like building a new housing society or setting up a new industry?” he told Al Jazeera.

Nizami also questioned how the proposed administrative units would sustain themselves economically.

“What will their economic model be? What will their growth model be? All of this is unclear right now,” he said.

The PPP, the PML-N’s main coalition partner nationally, governs Sindh. In September, the Sindh Assembly passed a resolution rejecting the province’s division.

President Asif Ali Zardari, the PPP’s cochairman, met Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in Lahore on Saturday.

Local media reported that Zardari reiterated the PPP’s opposition to dividing Sindh.

Shah said Sindh does not need new provinces and the PPP opposed a referendum because the constitution already set out the process. Other provinces, he said, could decide for themselves.

“If the Punjab Assembly has passed that provinces should be made there, then make them there. If the KP Assembly passed that provinces should be made there, then make provinces there,” he said.

Kamal, a former Karachi mayor, rejected that position. “Definitely Karachi should be an administrative unit. Karachi should be a provincial government,” he said in a recent interview with local media. Karachi, Pakistan’s largest city, is the MQM-P’s biggest stronghold.

The PML-N has no formal policy and said it would state its position when the matter reaches parliament. Malik, too, deferred to the party leadership.

“This matter remains the prerogative of the leadership of the party,” he told Al Jazeera.

Naqvi, meanwhile. has said no change will be made without coalition partners’ agreement. “If they all agree, everything will happen,” he said in Lahore.

articles.title: How is US Senate majority leader chosen?
articles.summary: Chris Van Hollen set to challenge Chuck Schumer for the post as the Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.
articles.body:
After the Democrats’ resounding success in this month’s midterm elections in the United States, attention is now turning to internal political battles as the party picks its new leaders in Congress.

With each new Congress, the parties each elect one member in the Senate and one in the House of Representatives to serve as their top leader in the two chambers. Depending on which party is in power, one party’s selections serve as majority leaders, the other as minority leaders. Leaders of both the Republican and Democratic caucuses also serve as the spokespeople for their parties’ positions on issues and coordinate their respective legislative strategies.

The parties choose these positions behind closed doors. However, to take up his or her post, the House speaker must win a vote in the full chamber on the day the new Congress first convenes, which will be January 3 this time around.

The election of the new Senate majority leader is set for early December although US media have reported efforts in the Democratic Party to try to fast-track the contest to avoid a divisive, drawn-out fight.

The Republican Party has already re-elected John Thune as their Senate leader for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. The election on the Democratic side, however, is shaping up to be more of a fight.

So who are the Senate majority leader candidates?

New York Senator Chuck Schumer, 75, has led the Democrats in the Senate since 2017. He was first elected to the chamber in 1999 and is now serving his fifth term. He served as minority leader from 2017 to 2021 and since 2025. He was majority leader from 2021 to 2025 during Joe Biden’s presidency.

Schumer has said he is confident he has the support within the party to be re-elected. However, since the November 3 midterms, his position has come under pressure from more left-wing Democrats who see him as too moderate.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is now in his second term in the Senate after representing his state in the House for 14 years. He became an early face of Democratic resistance to Trump during the president’s second term and launched his bid to succeed Schumer on Thursday , casting himself as a fresh face who reflected the public’s desire for change after the midterm elections.

Van Hollen was an early opponent of job and budget cuts carried out by the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency as many of those workers were based in Maryland.

He also drew widespread attention when he travelled to El Salvador to meet with imprisoned Maryland resident Kilmar Abrego Garcia , who was wrongly deported by the Trump administration and who federal courts said should be returned to the US.

Van Hollen has campaigned for accountability and transparency in the case of Al Jazeera journalist Shireen Abu Akleh , a Palestinian reporter and US citizen fatally shot by an Israeli soldier in 2022 while working in the occupied West Bank.

Van Hollen has received support from high-profile politicians, including Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders , an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed .

Schumer has fallen out of favour with more progressive members of the Democratic caucus. He notably backed El-Sayed’s primary opponent Haley Stevens.

He has been criticised for not opposing Trump’s agenda forcefully enough and has been accused of not doing enough to block Trump’s cabinet nominees from being confirmed by the Senate.

Schumer was chastised by those in his party, including California Governor Gavin Newsom, for “capitulating” to the Republicans during last year’s government shutdown and voting to reopen the government without securing any concessions in return.

However, many have credited Schumer with the turnaround in the Democrats’ political fortunes in this year’s elections and predicted that despite the discontent among progressives, he will prevail in the leadership election.

articles.title: Trump warns Iran about reported plot against admin officials: 'We take it very seriously'
articles.summary: Trump warned Iran would face unprecedented retaliation over a reported plot targeting Washington, D.C., as senior officials relocate to military housing.
articles.body: President Donald Trump warned Iran on Monday that it would face unprecedented retaliation if it were to carry out an attack on Washington, D.C. Trump made the statement in response to a report from CNN citing multiple U.S. officials stating that Iran is weighing an attempt at killing senior Trump administration officials by detonating a chemical weapon or a dirty bomb in the nation's capital. "Is there any imminent threat to Washington, D.C.?" a reporter asked on Monday. DHS CHIEF MULLIN SAYS IRAN POSES DAILY THREAT TO TRUMP AND HIS FAMILY AMID DRONE CONCERNS "Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before. I, I hope it's not, but it's — we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy. But this is why they can't have a nuclear weapon, by the way, in case people had any questions," Trump responded. Trump's statement came on the first leg of his trip across Asia this week, meeting with QUAD leaders in the Philippines on Monday, including Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. TRUMP KEEPS SIGNALING AN END TO IRAN WAR, BUT EXPERT WARNS A CRUCIAL PIECE OF HIS STRATEGY IS MISSING Trump said he plans to press Chinese President Xi Jinping to help end the war in Iran during their meeting later this week. CNN's report said Iran's plans for an attack on U.S. soil are in the preliminary phase and are, "for now, an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack." TRUMP ADMIN THREATENS IRAN WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' AS ALLIES CONVENE AMID THREATS OF POST-ELECTION ESCALATION White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told the outlet the U.S. is "monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland." The report comes days after news broke that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other senior U.S. officials were transferred to military housing in recent weeks. TRUMP'S TOP OFFICIALS RETREAT BEHIND MILITARY GATES AS EX-FBI DEPUTY POINTS TO WHAT'S FUELING THREATS Threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage" amid reported Iranian assassination threats, a senior administration official told Fox News Digital on Tuesday. The Iranian threats against Bessent come amid a documented history of alleged Tehran-backed assassination plots targeting senior U.S. officials. IRGC OPERATIVE LANDS ON FBI’S MOST WANTED TERRORISTS LIST OVER ALLEGED PLOT TO KILL FORMER TRUMP ADVISOR Attorney General Todd Blanche also relocated to a military base from his home around March, a different source familiar with the arrangements told Fox News Digital. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth have also reportedly taken up residence at Fort McNair in Washington, D.C., while White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other administration officials have moved to military installations or protected government housing. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The relocations have not all stemmed from the same threats. Some followed concerns about domestic political violence. Fox News' Ashley J. DiMella contributed to this report.

articles.title: Mullin took government plane to LSU-Texas football game with Americans stranded in wake of FAA outage: report
articles.summary: Secretary of State Markwayne Mullin reportedly flew a government plane to an LSU football game after the Federal Aviation Authority FAA lifted its ground stop.
articles.body: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin flew in a government plane to attend a college football game in Louisiana on Saturday, just one day after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop that continued to impact travelers through the weekend. Just 24 hours after Mullin stood next to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy at a White House podium to tell the nation why the FAA had issued a ground stop, prohibiting all planes from taking off, the Homeland chief was in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, to watch the Louisiana State University Tigers take on The University of Texas at Austin Longhorns, according to a report from the New York Post. Mullin, like other cabinet secretaries, cannot fly on commercial airliners due to safety concerns, so his trip was taken on a government plane, though government sources reportedly stressed to the Post that he paid for the travel expenses himself and that no special exceptions were made for the secretary. WAPO TRIES TO SHAME RUBIO'S USE OF MILITARY AIRCRAFT TO SEE SON'S FOOTBALL GAMES, HIS TEAM RESPONDS "Secretary Mullin is required by law to travel on a government airplane. This is to ensure access to secure communications and to comply by his constitutional duty of continuity of government should a national emergency arise," a Homeland Security spokesperson reportedly told the Post. "Any flight not related to his service as DHS Secretary he pays for personally," the spokesperson reportedly added. The Post also reported that Mullin spent at least part of the game in the private box of Ben Bordelon, the CEO of Louisiana-based shipping company Bollinger Shipyards. Bollinger has a number of government contracts, including a recently obtained $2.2 billion contract to build four icebreaking ships for the United States Coast Guard. "Secretary Mullin abides by all ethics requirements," a DHS spokesperson also told the Post. The LSU game was the second football game of the day for Mullin, who had also attended the Coast Guard Academy vs. the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy annual matchup at Audi Field in Washington, D.C., earlier on Saturday. PLAY SUNDAY OR FORFEIT: OKLAHOMA AD RIPS SEC COMMISSIONER OVER CONTROVERSIAL OLE MISS FAA SCHEDULING DECISION The previous evening, he had been shoulder to shoulder with Secretary Duffy, explaining to the nation that a technical glitch with a piece of FAA network infrastructure equipment likely prompted the systems failure that led to the ground stop. "What it appears to be right now is, as Secretary Duffy was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology and that new equipment, new technology, just wasn’t — it was overwhelming the older system," Mullin said Friday. FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP The ground stop ultimately lasted roughly five hours and impacted more than 1.5 million travelers on Friday alone. Despite the ground stop's lifting on Friday, travelers still felt the ripple effects through Monday.
